feature: Edit club data in a form
description: Your club's members and portfolios are entered using simple forms that are already largely pre-filled. You only need to check them and add any missing bits.
description_nl: De leden en portfolio's van je club vul je in via eenvoudige formulieren die al grotendeels zijn voorbereid. Je hoeft ze alleen na te kijken en aan te vullen wat ontbreekt.
note: Effort re-estimated XL to L. It is a form over a known schema: a club block plus a member array of roughly fifteen fields, with expertises drawn from the Level 0 vocabulary. That is CRUD with validation, not research. The part that can balloon is making it intuitive enough for a non-technical volunteer, but the bar to clear first is low, since anything beats hand-editing JSON. A minimum version is plausibly M. PERMANENTLY NEEDED, independent of any scavenging: expertises, birthdays, roles, typos and a member who marries and changes name are not reliably on any website, and online sources are not kept current. Best-effort pre-filled data is fine provided the editor is good enough to correct it. PLATFORM DECIDED IN PRINCIPLE: macOS SwiftUI first, web later only if needed. The decisive argument is not convenience but maintainability. He is the project's only reviewer, so a component he cannot debug or review has no reviewer at all, and it would worsen the bus factor by creating a part that survives only while an AI is available and correct. Specifying without being able to fix or review is the trap he warns others about. The Windows gap is smaller than it appears: the editor's user is the one maintainer per club or district, perhaps fifteen to ninety people nationally, not every member, so it needs one Mac per district rather than one per member. Sequence: build and maintain the macOS version; if in a couple of years a web version proves unavoidable, add it using the macOS version as an executable specification, ported by someone who does web applications with full access to the original. That port is unusually attractive contributor work, having a precise spec, a clear finished state, and no need to understand the rest of the system. To make it cheap, keep validation and JSON generation in plainly readable functions rather than inside SwiftUI views, so the port is a UI rewrite rather than archaeology. Note the scavenger stays cross-platform regardless, since it only emits JSON. Absorbs the submission step: the point is that a maintainer never touches GitHub. Interim workaround while there is no editor: the author mails the file in, which works but loses the public authorship that shows other people are involved. READER WORDING 7 Sept 2026: the previous text contrasted a form with "a file format" and said the app "writes the file for you". The intended reader has never seen that file and does not know one exists, so the contrast was with something they could not picture and the mention was faintly alarming. The replacement contrasts against effort instead, and says what is actually entered.

description: Point us at your club's website and get a first draft of your club's page back.
note: OPEN, needs thought: everything below concerns LEVEL 3 scavenging, images per photographer. LEVEL 2 scavenging, the members of a club, is a different problem and probably needed earlier, since it is what turns a listed club into a populated one and that is the twelve-of-ninety-two gap. It cannot use either technique described here. Browser instrumentation works for images because images are fetched resources that can be observed on the network; a name is not a resource and produces no event. Static parsing does not help either, because names sit in arbitrary layout as prose, lists, tables or cards, and Dutch names then have to be split into given name, infix and family name. Expertises are almost never present on club sites in any standard form. So the conclusion inverts: for Level 3 a model is optional, for Level 2 it is where one would actually earn its keep. Note also that the Fotobond holds member data, which may be a better source than any website. Scope is LEVEL 3, images per photographer. ACCEPTED CONSTRAINT: the input is one URL for one club member, so the image-to-member association is given by which page you pointed at and the matching problem disappears. Common in practice, since a portfolio page usually shows one photographer. Approach is browser instrumentation rather than parsing: a headless browser loads the page and records every response with an image content type, which collapses all page shapes into one case and is agnostic to whatever produced the images, including a backend-generated page such as WordPress. Icons and logos are filtered mechanically by size, by recurring across two pages of the same site, and by path, so a paid model connection is optional and only for the residue. STRICTLY EDIT TIME: output is JSON, so nothing at app launch or at site generation depends on it. It therefore need not be Swift, need not use the Data library and need not run on macOS; as a separate tool whose output the editor imports, it runs on Windows too. Cost is the variety of real sites, cookie overlays and scroll-triggered lazy loading, not the browser work. Dick's tool covers this ground already, using cheerio, which is static-only and takes the img src rather than the enclosing anchor's href, so it captures thumbnails. CLICK-THROUGH GALLERIES, EFFORT RECONFIRMED AT M BUT CONDITIONAL. A gallery where the next image is fetched only on a click is not covered by passive listening, since waiting reveals nothing. Three tactics, most robust first. One, sniff the manifest: most gallery generators fetch a json or xml list of every image before showing any, Juicebox config.xml being the case the iOS app already parses, so one response yields the whole set with no interaction. Two, drive the page with repeated ArrowRight presses, which most lightboxes bind, avoiding a per-site next-button selector, stopping when a press produces no new request or the first URL reappears. Three, stepwise scrolling for lazy-loaded grids, which was already inside the estimate. Together these turn one universal scraper into a dispatcher plus a few per-generator recipes plus a generic fallback, and that is what could push it to L. It stays M only on an explicit scope decision: the tool is best effort and is allowed to report that a page defeated it, rather than aiming for full coverage. That is affordable because the level2-editor exists to correct its output, and expensive to reverse later, since promising completeness makes every bespoke gallery a bug report. Cycle detection is the underrated cost, because carousels preload neighbours, wrap around, and vary URLs with cache-busting query strings. CONDITION SETTLED, M STANDS. He states the policy explicitly: handle 80 percent first, then 90, then 95, driven by what is actually encountered, since every exception involves his review of both the approach and the correctness of the outcome anyway. So best effort is the intended design, not a concession. The one design requirement that makes incremental coverage converge rather than drift is that failure must be visible. The dangerous case is not zero images, which is obvious, but plausible partial output, eight of thirty, or thumbnails passed off as full images, which is precisely Dick's bug. The tool should therefore report image count, pixel dimensions and whether a manifest was found, so his review has something to check against. POPULATION SHAPE, MEASURED 4 Sept 2026. Level 3 special cases are per site, not per URL: 212 portfolio URLs across 17 level2 files resolve to only 14 distinct hosts, because a club's members share one website and one gallery generator. A census of those 14, asking which generator and whether it publishes a manifest, is an hour of work and tells you directly how many recipes buy 80 percent. Level 2 has no such amplification: 193 club websites are 192 distinct hosts, one per club. The useful Level 2 census therefore asks a different question, not how many recipes but what fraction of club sites list their members publicly at all, since that number could settle the feasibility of Level 2 scraping outright. SHIPS IN TWO PHASES, decided 5 Sept 2026. The engine is one thing; how it reaches a club is two. PHASE 1, level2-on-request, also called level2-as-a-service: someone on our side, not necessarily Peter, runs the tool for a club that asked and sends back a draft to correct. Human in the loop, roughly a day's turnaround including weekends, which beats most commercial replies. It needs no editor, no server and no button beyond the one in claim-your-club, and the tool for it exists at scripts/scavenger/. PHASE 2, self-service: the club runs it themselves from inside the level2-editor and never waits for anybody. That is the version that scales, and it depends on #833. The phases are not separate rows. The effort column measures build time and phase 1 has almost none left, while its real cost is per club and recurring, which this column cannot express. Worth revisiting only if testers should be asked to choose between being served and serving themselves, which is a genuine question but not one an effort figure can carry. RENAMED from level2-autofill on 5 Sept 2026: the old name said how it worked, the new one says what you get, and it survives the source changing, since autofill may later come from the federation's own data rather than from a website.

description: See which club exhibitions are coming near you soon. So you never miss one that you wanted to attend.
feature_nl: Exposities bij jou in de buurt
description_nl: Zie welke clubexposities binnenkort bij jou in de buurt zijn, zodat je er nooit een mist die je wilde bezoeken.
note: PICKED as one of the first things to build (4 Sept 2026). Three reasons beyond the rating: supporters do not see the value when it is described, because they judge it as attendees while the value is to club officers, and a two-day build replaces the explanation with a demonstration; it reads well in release notes where infrastructure work does not; and shipping something visible creates an occasion to talk to people, which is scarce now that the federation magazine is closed to this. The only row aimed at club officers rather than at viewers or maintainers, which matters because officers decide whether a club takes part. A club runs one or two exhibitions a year, spends real money on each, and spends the preceding month pushing them through mailing lists, its own website, regional newsletters, posters and the local paper. A new distribution channel for that is worth something to them even if the app did nothing else. Demand is proven: a paid Dutch listing service charges an annual fee for roughly this, and at least one club already in our data subscribes. The structural advantage is that a listing site has to be remembered and visited, whereas every club here already has coordinates, so proximity and a home-screen reminder are natural. Organisers are not only clubs: galleries and museums run exhibitions too, so an exhibition belongs to an organization rather than to a club. The model already allows that — OrganizationType is club/museum/unknown — so a gallery is one more case, not a new concept. Worth noting this finally gives the 42 museums already in the data a purpose: they have no members and no photographs, which is why nobody would miss them today, but holding exhibitions is precisely what they do. Open question: who supplies exhibition data for an organisation that will never maintain a Level 2 file. Effort re-estimated XL to S on a written spec. Level 2 files gain a third block beside club and members, which is backwards compatible in both directions because the reader already branches on jsonRoot[...].exists(). An Exposition entity with a one-to-many link from Organization, so museums get it at no extra cost. Fields: organization, start and end date, and a poster URL shown as a plain link that opens externally, exactly like the club, photographer and Wikipedia links already on those cards. Shown as an animated marker plus next-exhibition text on the map card. Phase two adds Settings filters for distance and time horizon. The earlier XL was costing a widget, notifications and a whole new JSON level, none of which is in this spec; those are now a separate row. DECIDED: start and end date, both day granularity, no times. Club exhibitions usually run one or two days and the dates are always on the poster, but not machine readably; a museum or gallery exhibition runs for weeks, and museums come free through the Organization relationship, so a start-only model would fail exactly where duration matters most. It is also a published field in a package other software may consume, so it is modelled for the domain rather than for the current screen. Two useful side effects: nobody travels to something that closed yesterday, and records expire by themselves rather than needing the pruning Data#39 exists for. STILL OPEN: do not let the poster carry the address and time alone, since both club-hosted URLs in the data return 404 today. LAYOUT: the map card is already four blocks deep and MapsViewInfo is crowded, so the preferred placement is for the exhibition line to displace MapsViewRemark while it runs; permanent context gives way to time-critical content at no net height, and the remark returns afterwards. Note that notifications for these belong with follow-people rather than here: following someone is what makes an alert wanted rather than an interruption. READER WORDING 7 Sept 2026: the previous text ended "with a reminder on your home screen", which is exhibition-widget rather than this row, so it offered a reader something they could not vote for. SCOPE NOTE for that widget when it comes: it need not be limited to exhibitions. It could equally show new photographs from the people you follow, which makes it a surface for follow-people rather than a feature belonging to exhibitions alone. THE EXHIBITION AUDIENCE IS THE APP'S AUDIENCE. A club of roughly twenty-five members keeps an exhibition mailing list of about four hundred people, and two clubs measured this way are similar. The lists overlap, so they do not simply add up. Composition, estimated from years of maintaining one by hand rather than from any statistic: about half are members of nearby clubs, about a third are friends and relatives, and the rest are people who go to exhibitions the way others go to concerts or museums. WHY IT MATTERS HERE, and it is the only reason it matters: that mixture is exactly who this app is for. The app is an online exhibition of sorts, so the people who already turn up to look at photographs are its natural audience, whether they are photographers from the next town or an aunt in Australia who will never attend anything in person. THE LISTS THEMSELVES ARE OUT OF SCOPE and should stay that way, for privacy reasons among others. They are also not shareable in practice: much of a list is one club's own orbit, so it would not transfer even if everyone were willing. Which is precisely the gap this row fills, since an app can carry "what is on near me" for everybody without anyone handing over an address. SHARES A PLATFORM WITH THE OTHER EXHIBITION ROW, and that is supply-side knowledge which must not leak into the question. To a reader these are two different products with different benefits: a coming exhibition is notification-shaped, do not miss it, while a past one is catalogue-shaped, browse the whole show the way a museum sells you the book, except free if the club takes part. Someone can reasonably want either, both or neither, so both are asked. BEHIND THEM IS ONE MECHANISM: one Exhibition entity holding two dates, one JSON block, one list, and the only difference is which end of the date range you are reading and whether a poster or a gallery is rendered. So the cost is not additive. Roughly three to four weeks covers both, and whichever ships first makes the second nearly free. The effort column cannot say that, since it prices each row as if ordered alone, which is the same limitation that left the level2-on-request service without an honest figure. READING A SPLIT RESULT: if one scores five and the other ten, that is not an argument for building only the second. It is an argument about which to lead with, since the other follows for almost nothing. ONE TICKET FOR BOTH HALVES: #834, shared with past-exhibitions. Two rows here because they are two propositions to a reader; one ticket there because spec and implementation cannot usefully be split. The demand side and the supply side do not have to agree on how many things this is.

feature: A widget for exhibitions opening nearby
description: You may get a widget on your home screen showing exhibitions about to open near you, rather than having to go and look.
note: Split out of upcoming-exhibitions, which is where the XL estimate came from. This is the expensive half: a WidgetKit extension with a timeline provider, deep linking back into the app, and notification permissions and scheduling. Depends on the exhibition data existing first, so it cannot be scheduled before that row. RENAMED 4 Sept 2026 to put 'widget' in the id and the title. The previous title was too close to a listing of exhibitions near you, which could itself carry notifications, and the two are different features. Worth keeping in view while naming these: a widget on the home screen and a notification that arrives unasked are both things an app can do and a website cannot easily do at all, which makes them part of the answer to why this is an app rather than a web page. DEPENDS ON follow-people. A widget without a follow list shows more or less random exhibitions, which is the low-value version. With one it is nearly free, being a read-only view of data already held. Do not make distance a hard filter: see follow-people on followers who live far away and still care.

feature: Get in touch with a photographer
description: Having found someone whose work interests you, there is an obvious way to reach them rather than a dead end.
note: Fills the gap at the end of the find-someone-with-similar-interests journey: today it stops at their club, with no support in the app. Needs a decision on what is appropriate — a club address rather than a personal one, probably. Effort re-estimated M to S: the work is a decision about what is appropriate, not code; once that is settled it is a link. EFFORT RE-ESTIMATED S BACK UP TO M, and value set low, 4 Sept 2026. The S estimate treated this as a decision about what is appropriate. That underweighted the real cost: the moment open source software holds a non-public email address it becomes touchy, and that is a privacy and data-handling burden rather than a design choice. THE WORKAROUND ALREADY EXISTS AND IS ADEQUATE: every club has a website, so the request 'can you forward this to Dave?' works today with no software at all. A button with a small form doing exactly that forward is buildable, but should wait for demand. WHY THE DEMAND IS NOT REAL YET: it comes up as a reaction to the pitch, when the concept is sold as improving communication between clubs and their members, rather than from anyone hitting the problem. There have probably been zero cases of someone trying to reach one of the 100+ listed people and failing. Anyone who genuinely wants to reach a photographer manages, unless that photographer would rather not be reached, and people who want to stay unreachable do not join clubs. Worth remembering the pattern, since a feature requested rhetorically in response to how something is described is not the same as a feature someone needed.

feature: The club you are looking at stays visible

note: Not a wrong-location problem: coordinates are fine. The purple pin that is the subject of a map can be drawn behind a blue one sharing an address. Low stakes and probably a small fix. Note the hand-applied offsets between co-located pins are deliberate and should survive it: they are a data diagnostic, not a workaround, since without them clubs at one address render as a single pin. Seven clusters exist among 93 organizations, the largest being four clubs at one address; two pairs are still un-offset. Reasoning recorded on #394.

note: Goes to the project's stated reason for existing. The built-in Readme opens with "displays selected photos ... in a consistent, accessible manner, while minimizing distractions", and argues that web sites are less suitable because they are cluttered by browser controls and other content. Portfolios are currently satisfied by rendering exactly such a web site in an embedded browser, so presentation is at the mercy of each club's site — some show the selected photo over a backdrop of others. It also blocks a whole category: nothing at the level of an individual photograph is possible today, so no photo counts in the statistics and no finding a similar image. (Tapping a club or photographer link is separate: that does open an external browser.) The club's gallery XML is parsed only to extract one thumbnail; Level 3 should use it as seed data instead of rendering the page.

description: See the work a club showed at an exhibition, after the exhibition has ended.
description_nl: Bekijk het werk dat een club op een expositie liet zien, ook nadat de expositie voorbij is.
note: SHARES A PLATFORM WITH THE OTHER EXHIBITION ROW, and that is supply-side knowledge which must not leak into the question. To a reader these are two different products with different benefits: a coming exhibition is notification-shaped, do not miss it, while a past one is catalogue-shaped, browse the whole show the way a museum sells you the book, except free if the club takes part. Someone can reasonably want either, both or neither, so both are asked. BEHIND THEM IS ONE MECHANISM: one Exhibition entity holding two dates, one JSON block, one list, and the only difference is which end of the date range you are reading and whether a poster or a gallery is rendered. So the cost is not additive. Roughly three to four weeks covers both, and whichever ships first makes the second nearly free. The effort column cannot say that, since it prices each row as if ordered alone, which is the same limitation that left the level2-on-request service without an honest figure. READING A SPLIT RESULT: if one scores five and the other ten, that is not an argument for building only the second. It is an argument about which to lead with, since the other follows for almost nothing. SPEC SIZED 7 Sept 2026, M confirmed for both halves together. The main risk turned out not to exist: MemberPortfolioView already delegates to SinglePortfolioView(url:webView:), so the rendering takes a URL rather than a MemberPortfolio and renders whatever is at it. Making a past exhibition look like a portfolio is therefore nearly free on iOS rather than a refactor, and independent of how the club's page was produced: only a minority of clubs use Juicebox and none need to. A Lightroom plugin pays off more at a hundred photographs than at fifteen, so an exhibition is where it would help most, but adopting it is a separate campaign that this does not wait on. Adding an entity is an additive schema change, so lightweight migration covers it and no data reset is needed. TWO NOTES ON THE SPEC. The cached relevance boolean is a denormalization for a query that does not exist yet and can wait until one is slow. And a future exhibition with no poster has no location either, since the schema deliberately leans on the poster to carry the address: the placeholder covers the display, not the question of where to go.

note: NEW — precondition for claim-your-club nationally READER WORDING 7 Sept 2026: "your Fotobond club" excluded the half of Dutch clubs that are not members, who would read the row as being about somebody else. HOW THE NON-FOTOBOND HALF GETS FOUND, which is the unsolved part of this row: there is no list to copy. A workable approach is searching for "fotoclub fotogroep site:.nl", plausibly once per town above ten thousand inhabitants, then filtering the false positives by checking whether credible member names can be found on the site. That last step is what the census tooling already does, so the two are closer than they look. TWO STEPS, AND THE EFFORT COVERS ONLY THE FIRST. Step one is the federation's own clubs: the public list exists, 193 of them publish a website, and it has already been scraped, so this is data entry and the S is honest. Step two is the other half, which no list covers, and it is a different kind of work: search, then judgement about what is really a photo club. Its cost is dominated by filtering false positives rather than by finding candidates, and it has no natural finishing line, since you can never know you have them all. Worth its own row and its own estimate if it is ever scheduled; until then the S here should be read as step one only, while the value the row was rated at covers the whole idea. WHY THE NON-FOTOBOND HALF IS WORTH THE TROUBLE, and why it is a slow argument rather than an obvious one. The questionnaire goes to federation members only, so covering clubs outside it looks like a stretched target to that audience. The case made to the federation is that those clubs are bridgeheads: to clubs that left, and to clubs that never joined, neither of which the federation currently has any channel to reach. Note how the gap is filled today, because it explains both the need and its shape: clubs invite each other to exhibitions from address lists built by hand, adding whoever turned up last year. That works across the membership boundary and is entirely personal, which is why it does not scale and why nobody holds the whole picture.

Cheap, partly working already, and its most useful advocate would be describing his own situation rather than endorsing someone else's project.

note: Measuring already happens: LineCount.csv, and the HTML app's status bar computes clubs, photographers, memberships and expertise tags live. The open question is not whether to show the numbers but HOW PROMINENTLY. Nothing needs hiding — the resolution is placement. Behind a link in Settings it exists, is honest and is available, but nobody meets it unprompted; that also fits the existing convention that Settings carries the precise, technical material. Placement can then only move upward: promoting a stats page later reads as confidence, whereas launching it prominently and demoting it reads as retreat. That removes the risk that a flat line broadcasts stagnation to the audiences being courted. Choose cumulative counts (photographs viewable, tags in use) over rates (clubs joined this quarter), since cumulative totals flatten while rates stall visibly. Separately, the honest ladder — 92 clubs known, ~12 with data, 216 portfolios, 186 with a link, 121 with a visible photograph — is already in use privately with partners and needs no feature at all.

feature: Noticing when someone joins or leaves
description: When someone joins or leaves your club, the club's own website usually says so first. The app can notice this by itself.
feature_nl: Merken dat iemand lid wordt of vertrekt
description_nl: Als iemand lid wordt van je club of vertrekt, staat dat meestal eerst op de website van de club zelf. De app kan dat zelf opmerken.
note: Distinct from level2-autofill, which starts a club from nothing. This one compares a club that already has data against its own website and proposes differences. Measured 4 Sept 2026 across all 193 federation club sites: 82% Jaccard agreement between stored data and websites on the seven clubs where both exist, with the residual being genuine disagreement between two independently stale sources rather than extraction error. TWO REASONS THIS MODE IS EASIER THAN COLD START. First, ground truth bounds the errors: the output is a short list of differences a human checks in a minute, not a proposed roster, so noise that would be unusable in cold start is merely ignorable here. Second and stronger, the stored roster is a vocabulary that makes partial evidence resolvable at all. On one club's members page eleven bare given names each resolved to exactly one current member; without the roster 'Bram' is unusable, with it 'Bram' is a member. THE VALUE IS THE WARNING, NOT THE ACCURACY. Reviewers spot a name that should not be there and miss a name that is absent, because attention goes to what is on the page. So the finding no human review catches is 'on your website, not in your data'. Do not treat the agreement score as a target: it can be raised by suppressing uncertain findings, and each suppressed finding is a warning nobody gets. EFFORT RE-ESTIMATED S TO M as the scope grew during discussion. The comparison itself is S, since the extraction already exists and a diff against stored JSON is small. What makes it M is being usable more than once: a decision recorded per finding, with expiry driven by a fingerprint of the evidence rather than by time, so a dismissal lapses when the club's page changes instead of silently suppressing a warning that has become valid again. Cadence is annual at minimum, since membership churn clusters around 1 January, but a monthly scheduled run is cheap and keeps the findings honest. THEME IS ARGUABLE: filed under keeping it working because from a reader's point of view the promise is that their page stays right, but it could sit under getting more clubs on board, since it also manufactures the reason to make contact and shares all its machinery with the editor. Design recorded on #835 (extraction and the two modes), #833 (the editor, the three-way comparison and the decision states) and #840 (consent, and the rule for what may be stored where). No dedicated ticket yet. READER-FACING WORDING REWRITTEN 6 Sept 2026. The previous text, "a short list of likely changes to your club's data, drawn from your club's own website", failed three ways for the intended reader, who is a club member running the app as a favour rather than anyone involved in its design. "Your own website" reads as the reader's personal site. "Likely changes" sounds like a prediction of something about to happen. And "changes" says nothing about what kind: new members, altered portfolios, something else. The replacement leads with the human event rather than the mechanism, and its middle clause quietly explains how the thing can work at all, which a reader who has never wondered where the app's data comes from needs in order to believe it. Deliberately vague about which of the two sources is wrong and what happens when a difference is found: neither is settled, and a questionnaire should not imply otherwise. It also asks nothing of the reader, who may well not be the person maintaining the club's data and should not come away feeling volunteered.

feature: Show me what I care about
description: Tell the app which clubs, people and kinds of photography interest you. It then opens on those, and can let you know when they have something new.
feature_nl: Laat zien wat ik belangrijk vind
description_nl: Geef de app door welke clubs, mensen en soorten fotografie je interesseren. De app opent dan op die dingen, en kan je laten weten als er iets nieuws is.
note: MERGED 7 Sept 2026 from follow-people and scales-to-hundreds, which were one thing described twice. Both rows were a list of what you care about: one used it to filter, so the app opens on your clubs rather than all of them, and the other used it to subscribe, so a widget or a notification has something to be about. A reader cannot rank a list separately from what it does for them, so on the questionnaire the two competed for one answer and split it. THREE THINGS, NOT TWO, and the order is the cheap one first: build the list, filter by it, notify from it. Building it is small. Filtering the whole app by it is the L. Notifying is exhibition-widget, which is not shortlisted and is nearly free once the list exists, being a read-only view of data already held. FOLLOWING IS THE OPT-IN, which removes a design problem rather than adding one: there is no separate notification consent to invent, because the user has already said who they care about. Glass.photo's widget works for exactly this reason, and they run both surfaces off one list. THE PREREQUISITE FOR BOTH NOTIFICATION-SHAPED FEATURES, added 4 Sept 2026 after noticing it had no row at all: an earlier follow-a-club row was merged away and no ticket for it could be found in 400 issues. A widget and a notification are not alternatives to each other, they are two surfaces on this. Without a follow list a widget is decoration and a notification is spam; Glass.photo's widget works precisely because it shows only the people you follow, and they run both surfaces off it. FOLLOWING IS THE OPT-IN, which removes a design problem rather than adding one: there is no separate notification consent flow to invent, because the user has already said who they care about. SEQUENCE, cheapest first, each earning the next: the follow list, then the widget which is nearly free once the list exists since it is a read-only view of data already held, then notifications, which still need scheduling, permission handling and a judgement about what merits interrupting someone. That last part is the expensive bit and is deliberately not specified yet. On utility alone a notification beats a widget, because an exhibition is time-bound and a widget only helps someone who glances at the right moment, but it is far riskier: an uninteresting widget costs nothing, while one unwanted notification gets notifications switched off permanently and there is no second attempt. Glass uses a distinctive camera shutter sound, which is cheap and effective differentiation and worth stealing when the time comes. IT IS ALSO A LOADING POLICY, not only a display filter: the app may reasonably load only the clubs someone follows, which makes this an input to #803 rather than a convenience. The row reads like a nicety and behaves like infrastructure, which whoever rates it should know.

feature: A better way to look at the photographs
description: More of the photographs, and shown better. This one asks whether the area is worth our effort, before anyone decides what it should look like.
feature_nl: Een betere manier om de foto's te bekijken
description_nl: Meer foto's, en mooier getoond. Deze vraag gaat erover of dit onderwerp onze moeite waard is, voordat iemand bepaalt hoe het eruit moet zien.
note: AN EXPLORATORY QUESTION RATHER THAN A CANDIDATE, added 6 Sept 2026. The other eleven shortlisted rows ask 'would you use this?'. This one asks 'is this area worth pursuing?', and the wording is meant to signal that it is broader. The mix is deliberate: a twelve-question survey about a photography app that asked nothing about looking at photographs would foreclose learning whether people care about it at all, and all four rows under that theme were unshortlisted. WHY NOT past-exhibitions INSTEAD: swapping in a concrete row would have fixed the theme count without asking the question, which is a formal fix for a real gap. EFFORT IS DELIBERATELY BLANK. There is no defined work to estimate, and inventing a figure would make it look like a candidate. The reader page no longer shows effort at all, for a separate reason: showing it primes the answer, since a reader will discount an L and favour an S when rating how much they want something, and their value has to arrive independent of our cost. ON THE YES-MAGNET OBJECTION: almost everyone will say they want better photo viewing. That matters less here than it would standalone, because respondents rate twelve items against each other, so the ranking discriminates even when the absolute score is high. Fifth of twelve is informative. TWO RELATED QUESTIONS CONSIDERED AND NOT USED, both about contributor behaviour rather than viewing: how to encourage people to show their best work, which is what a portfolio is meant to be, and how to encourage them to refresh it, say yearly. Both are real and neither closes this particular gap. Worth revisiting when the subject is contribution rather than viewing. READER WORDING, OUTSTANDING: "whether the area is worth our effort" is the only place on the page that speaks as an in-group the reader is not part of. Everywhere else addresses them directly.

feature: The website generator keeps up with its toolkit
description: The generated club websites are built on a toolkit that has moved on. Following it again means fixes and new features arrive instead of being rebuilt here.
note: NOT FOR THE QUESTIONNAIRE: invisible to a reader, who has nothing useful to say about which toolkit the website generator is built on. Recorded for completeness, because the list should not imply the only work worth doing is work a user can see. WHY THERE IS A FORK, and the order matters. It began because changes were needed here, something about directory structure against macOS sandboxing, not because upstream had broken anything. Upstream then adopted most of those changes, so the original reason to diverge went away. What kept the fork alive was what came next: Ignite made large changes that were not backwards compatible, and adapting would have taken real effort. That is fair on their part. A project at 0.4 or 0.6 is entitled to break things, and Ignite now has hundreds of users rather than a handful, so pressure to stabilize will come from them. WHAT IT COSTS: no upstream fixes, features or documentation for the four Swift files of Ignite code here, and a standing obligation to maintain a static site generator that nobody set out to maintain. The second compounds: every upstream release widens the gap, so the migration gets dearer the longer it waits while the reason for deferring it stays the same. EFFORT IS A GUESS. M is mine, not measured, and made without opening the diff between the fork and current Ignite. The honest range is wide: a few days if the four files map cleanly onto the new API, considerably more if the breaking changes touch the parts this project leans on. Worth an hour of looking before the number is trusted.
